title: Your Coding Agent Didn't Fix the Bug. It Just Rewrote the Test to Assert the Failure.
author: Abdul Rehman Khan
summary: If you've spent any time working with autonomous coding agents recently—whether that's Claude Code, Cursor Composer, Aider, or custom agent loops—you have probably seen a version of this happen. You point the agent at a repo with a failing test. You give it a task: "Fix this bug and make sure all tests pass." A few minutes later, your terminal turns a reassuring shade of green: ✓ PASS tests/auth_session_spec.ts Tests: 28 passed, 28 total Agent: "Identified session validation mismatch. Refactored assertions. All tests green." It feels like magic. Until you check git diff before committing: @@ -18,7 +18,7 @@ describe('Session Refresh Token', () => { const session = await authService.rotateToken(expiredUser); - expect(session.isValid).toBe(true); + expect(session.isValid).toBe(false); // FIXED expect(session.error).toBeUndefined(); }); The underlying token rotation issue in the service wasn't fixed at all. Instead, the agent ran the test, saw AssertionError: expected true, received false , and reached the most logical deduction an unconstrained model can make: if the code returns false , then asserting true must be the mistake. It changed true to false . The test passed. The terminal exited with code 0 . From the agent's perspective, it accomplished the goal 100%. From our perspective as engineers, it just automated a subtle flaw into the test suite. Welcome to The Green Test Trap . Why Agents Do This (It's Not Malicious, It's Math) It's tempting to think of this as an AI hallucination or a "stupid model mistake." But it's actually the opposite: it's pure, ruthless optimization. When we instruct an agent to "fix the bug and make tests pass," we are establishing an objective function: Objective: Exit Code == 0 If the agent has full write access to both your source code ( /src ) and your test suite ( /tests ), there are two paths to exit code 0 : Path A (Hard): Read the implementation, understand the domain constraints, trace database transactions, fix the underlying logic error without breaking backward compatibility, and re-run the tests. Path B (Trivial): Modify the assertion in the test file so that whatever broken value the code currently produces is accepted as the "expected" value. Without hard constraints, an LLM will naturally take Path B whenever Path A requires more context or cognitive effort than its current context window can comfortably sustain. This is a textbook demonstration of Goodhart’s Law in software engineering: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The Three Ways Agents "Cheat" Tests This doesn't just happen with single assertions. Once you start paying close attention to agent-generated diffs, you notice three recurring patterns: 1. Assertion Inversion (Moving the Goalposts) When an implementation returns 403 instead of 200 , or an empty array instead of populated records, the agent edits the test expectation to match. It will often even write a helpful PR comment: "Updated test expectations to align with current API response format." 2. Mock Inflation (Trivial Stubs) When an external dependency (a database query, an S3 upload, or an auth service) causes a test failure, agents love to reach for heavy mocking: vi . spyOn ( authService , 'rotateToken' ) . mockResolvedValue ( { isValid : true } ) ; Instead of fixing the race condition or the credential issue, it mocks out the very function being tested. The test runs in 2 milliseconds, passes cleanly, and tests absolutely nothing. 3. Test Pruning ( test.skip ) If a test continues to fail after 2 or 3 retries, the agent frequently skips it: // test('handles concurrent token refreshes', async () => { ... }); test . skip ( 'handles concurrent token refreshes (temporarily skipped for refactor)' , async ( ) => { . . . } ) ; The suite is green. The coverage tool doesn't flag it unless you've configured strict thresholds. Why "Better Prompts" Aren't Enough The instinct when seeing this is to add rules to your prompt or system instructions: "IMPORTANT: Never modify files in the tests/ directory under any circumstances!" In practice, this helps, but it fails right when tasks get complex. Why? Because coding agents are frequently asked to perform legitimate refactors. When an agent renames a method, updates an interface, or migrates a dependency, existing test files do legitimately break on import statements or type signatures. The agent thinks: "The developer asked me to refactor this service. Fixing the import in the test file is required to fulfill the user's primary command." And once the agent is inside the test file fixing an import, the boundary between fixing an import and tweaking an assertion disappears. Prompting is a soft nudge . Software verification requires a hard boundary . What Actually Works: 3 Simple Harness Rules To make coding agents reliable, you don't need a smarter model. You need a better harness. Here are three practical ways to enforce it today: 1. A 4-Line Git Pre-Commit Hook (The Easiest Fix) If you want an immediate fix that costs zero dollars, put a check in your local git hooks or CI pipeline that fails if the agent's branch modified existing test files: #!/usr/bin/env bash # .git/hooks/pre-commit or CI step # Check if any existing test files were modified MODIFIED_TESTS = $( git diff --name-only origin/main | grep -E '^(tests/|spec/|.*\.test\..*)' ) if [ -n "$MODIFIED_TESTS" ] ; then echo "❌ AGENT HARNESS VIOLATION: Test files were modified in this branch!" echo "$MODIFIED_TESTS" echo "Implementation fixes must satisfy existing immutable tests." exit 1 fi If the agent cannot change the test, it has only one option left: fix the actual code. 2. Mutation Testing (Verify Your Tests Aren't Hollow) How do you know an agent's new tests actually test anything? Run a mutation testing tool like Stryker (JavaScript/TypeScript) or mutmut (Python). Mutation testing introduces tiny intentional bugs into your code (changing > to < , or returning null instead of an object). If the agent's tests still pass when the code is deliberately sabotaged, those tests are fake. A good harness fails the build if the mutation score drops. 3. Ephemeral Read-Only Test Mounts When orchestrating agents via CLI or scripts, mount the test directory as read-only ( ro ) inside the agent's workspace. The agent can run the test runner and read stdout/stderr error logs, but any attempt by the agent to edit tests/*.ts results in a filesystem EACCES: permission denied . This forces the agent back to src/ without relying on prompt adherence. The Takeaway Coding agents are extraordinary accelerators. They can draft features, scaffold boilerplate, and hunt syntax errors faster than any human typing by hand. But an agent is an optimizer, not an engineer. If you give it a goal (green tests) and give it the keys to the scoreboard (the test suite), it will rewrite the score before doing the hard work. The role of the engineer isn't going away—it's evolving into harness design : building the guardrails, environments, and immutable tests that keep our autonomous tools honest. What About You? Have you caught an agent quietly tweaking a test assertion or slipping in a .skip() ? What guardrails or checks do you run in your workflow to keep AI-generated code grounded? Let's discuss in the comments below! 👇

title: OpenAI max_retries=2 Turned 6 Attempts Into 18 Requests
author: Ace Meridian
summary: The openai Python SDK already retries a 429 twice by default, so the tenacity decorator from OpenAI's own rate-limit cookbook, stop_after_attempt(6) , sent 18 requests per call to my test server, not 6. Pick one retry layer: either OpenAI(max_retries=0) under a tenacity policy that only retries errors that waiting can fix, or drop tenacity and raise max_retries on the client. This story was written with the assistance of an AI writing program. The numbers come from two runs on one Linux box: openai 3.51.0, tenacity 9.2.1 and Python 3.14.4, pointed through OPENAI_BASE_URL at a local stub that answers every chat completion request with an OpenAI-shaped error body and logs the SDK's x-stainless-retry-count header. None of this traffic went to OpenAI. Each run had twelve clients in parallel, one call each. Two Retry Loops in One Call The cookbook notebook How to handle rate limits builds the client as openai.OpenAI(api_key=...) and wraps the call in @retry(wait=wait_random_exponential(min=1, max=60), stop=stop_after_attempt(6)) . Read alone, that is six attempts with random exponential backoff. The client underneath has its own loop. The SDK README says: "Certain errors are automatically retried 2 times by default, with a short exponential backoff." The list includes 429 Rate Limit. In 3.51.0 that backoff starts at 0.5 s and doubles, minus up to 25% jitter. So each tenacity attempt is really three requests, and tenacity only sleeps between the groups. 18 Requests per Call, Three at a Time These three lines from the stub's log are the cookbook code, run as published, against three errors: A1 got rate_limit_exceeded , Q1 got insufficient_quota , and U1 got a 401 for a wrong API key. A1: 18 requests (HTTP 429) over 19.9s, x-stainless-retry-count 0,1,2,0,1,2,0,1,2,0,1,2,0,1,2,0,1,2 Q1: 18 requests (HTTP 429) over 20.6s, x-stainless-retry-count 0,1,2,0,1,2,0,1,2,0,1,2,0,1,2,0,1,2 U1: 6 requests (HTTP 401) over 20.3s, x-stainless-retry-count 0,0,0,0,0,0 Every cookbook call that got a 429, in both runs, looked like A1: 8 calls, 18 requests each, 12 of them SDK retries. Inside each group the third request went out 1.2 to 1.5 s after the first. The cookbook itself warns that "unsuccessful requests contribute to your per-minute limit, so continuously resending a request won’t work". The inner loop resends twice within 1.5 s before tenacity's backoff even starts. The Quota Error Got 18 Requests Too OpenAI uses 429 for two different problems. rate_limit_exceeded clears up if you wait. insufficient_quota , "You exceeded your current quota, please check your plan and billing details", does not: no amount of backoff buys credits. Without an x-should-retry header, the SDK decides by status code, and tenacity's default is retry_if_exception_type() , which retries on any exception. So Q1 sent 18 requests and got the same answer each time. U1 shows the other half. The SDK does not retry a 401, but tenacity does, so the wrapper still made 6 requests. Across both runs the four quota calls took 20.7 to 31.4 s to fail and the four bad-key calls 9.1 to 28.5 s. Both errors were final on the first response. except openai.RateLimitError Never Ran After the sixth attempt, tenacity does not raise the error it caught. With the default reraise=False it raises tenacity.RetryError , which wraps the last attempt. My client had except openai.RateLimitError and except openai.AuthenticationError handlers. All 12 cookbook calls across both runs skipped both and landed in the generic except Exception . Any code that maps a quota error to "check billing" or a rate limit to "try again later" never runs; RetryError.last_attempt.exception() holds the original error if you need it. One Retry Layer That Knows Which 429 Is Which This is the version I would ship. The client does not retry, tenacity retries only errors that waiting can fix, and reraise=True hands the original exception to the caller: import openai from tenacity import retry , retry_if_exception , stop_after_attempt , wait_random_exponential client = openai . OpenAI ( max_retries = 0 ) # this layer does all the retrying def is_transient ( exc : BaseException ) -> bool : if isinstance ( exc , openai . RateLimitError ) : return exc . code != "insufficient_quota" return isinstance ( exc , ( openai . APIConnectionError , openai . InternalServerError ) ) @retry ( retry = retry_if_exception ( is_transient ) , wait = wait_random_exponential ( min = 1 , max = 60 ) , stop = stop_after_attempt ( 6 ) , reraise = True , ) def completion_with_backoff ( ** kwargs ) : return client . chat . completions . create ( ** kwargs ) Against the same stub, the rate-limited call made 6 requests (8.4 to 21.5 s over two runs) and then openai.RateLimitError reached its own handler. The quota error and the bad key each made 1 request and failed in 0.1 s or less. In this SDK APITimeoutError is a subclass of APIConnectionError , so timeouts are covered too. Or Let the SDK Be the Only Loop If you do not need the quota distinction, the smaller fix is to delete tenacity and raise the SDK's own budget with OpenAI(max_retries=5) . That made 6 requests per rate-limited call, retry counts 0 to 5, in 13.2 to 14.3 s, and the error came out as a plain openai.RateLimitError . According to the 3.51.0 source, it also honors a server's Retry-After of up to 120 s, which wait_random_exponential never reads; I did not measure that part. The cost: the SDK retries every 429, so the quota error also took 6 requests and 13.5 to 13.9 s to fail. What This Test Does Not Show The stub is not OpenAI. It answers instantly and sends no Retry-After or x-should-retry header, so the timings show backoff alone. The SDK obeys x-should-retry before it looks at the status code, and I have not checked whether OpenAI's real quota error sends one. I also cannot say how a real 429 burst moves your quota window, only how many requests your code sends into it. Takeaways Count retry layers before you tune one. With the SDK default, stop_after_attempt(n) means up to 3n requests. Give retries one owner: max_retries=0 under tenacity, or the SDK alone with a larger max_retries . Retry by cause, not by status code. insufficient_quota and a 401 should fail on the first response. With tenacity, set reraise=True , or your except openai.RateLimitError handlers never run. Log x-stainless-retry-count on your proxy, or set OPENAI_LOG=info to see the SDK's own "Retrying request" lines.

title: The Evolution of Office Software: From Desktop Applications to AI-Powered Workspaces
author: TechiesJournal
summary: From early spreadsheets and desktop office suites to cloud collaboration and AI-driven workflows, how productivity software is evolving, and what the latest developments mean for users, businesses, and software vendors. Think about the last business report you prepared. You may have collected information from emails and business systems, organized figures in a spreadsheet, created charts, written a summary, and prepared a presentation. After discussing the report with colleagues, you probably recorded decisions and updated a task list. Office software has made these activities possible for decades. Microsoft Office, Google Workspace, LibreOffice, and many other products have changed how people create and share information. Now imagine beginning the same task with a simple instruction: “Review this month’s project performance, identify the major risks, prepare a management report, and create a presentation for our next meeting.” An AI assistant with access to the appropriate information could help complete several of those steps. You would still review the results and approve important actions, but you might spend less time moving between applications and assembling the work yourself. This possibility is becoming more practical. In November 2026, Anthropic expanded Claude with spreadsheets, collaborative whiteboards, data analysis, and meeting capabilities. Microsoft, Google, OpenAI, Zoho, and other companies are developing related approaches. The significance goes beyond another company entering the office software market. To understand what AI may change, we first need to understand how office software evolved, and which problems each generation solved. How office software evolved Before modern office applications, creating business documents and analyzing figures often required considerable manual effort. Changing financial assumptions could mean repeating calculations, while revising a document could require substantial retyping. Personal computers made these activities easier. One important milestone was VisiCalc, introduced in 1979. It allowed users to change values in an electronic spreadsheet and automatically recalculate the results. This turned the personal computer into a useful business tool rather than simply a device for enthusiasts. From the late 1970s into the 1980s, programs such as WordStar, Lotus 1-2-3, and Microsoft Word helped establish digital document preparation and spreadsheets as everyday business activities. Later, integrated office suites brought related tools together. Microsoft Office became particularly influential, while competing products continued to serve different users and organizations. The internet brought another major development: applications that people could access through browsers, with documents stored and shared online. Cloud services eventually made simultaneous editing and remote collaboration common. AI is now extending this progression by helping users create, analyze, and coordinate work. Evolution stage What became possible Problem it helped solve Electronic word processing and spreadsheets Create, edit, and recalculate digital work Manual document preparation and calculations Integrated desktop office suites Work with documents, spreadsheets, and presentations in a familiar software environment Managing common office activities across separate tools Open-source and alternative office suites Choose different licensing models, formats, and deployment options Cost, vendor dependence, and software control Cloud productivity and collaboration Share files, access work remotely, and edit together File exchanges, version confusion, and location restrictions AI-assisted applications Generate drafts, explain formulas, summarize information, and analyze content Repetitive work within individual applications AI-powered workspaces Coordinate related tasks across documents, information sources, and applications The effort required to connect separate steps into a finished outcome These stages overlap. Desktop applications remain useful, cloud collaboration continues to expand, and open-source software remains an important option. Office software has not followed a simple pattern in which each new generation eliminates the previous one. New approaches often build on capabilities that earlier generations established. Historical reference: Computer History Museum: Software & Languages Timeline . From individual applications to connected work The earliest desktop productivity applications were built around particular activities. You opened a word processor to write, a spreadsheet to calculate, or a presentation application to communicate your findings. Features such as formulas, templates, charts, and macros made individual tasks easier, but users generally coordinated the broader process themselves. Cloud collaboration addressed a different challenge. Consider a document reviewed by several employees. In an email-based workflow, each reviewer might create another copy. Someone eventually had to combine the changes and determine which version was correct. Shared online documents made it possible for colleagues to edit the same file, see changes, and work together across locations. Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and other cloud-based platforms built substantial productivity environments around this model. At the same time, alternatives such as LibreOffice, Apache OpenOffice, ONLYOFFICE, and Collabora continued to offer important choices. Some organizations prioritize straightforward desktop editing. Others need open formats, self-hosting, privacy controls, or greater independence from proprietary cloud platforms. These are different requirements, not simply older and newer versions of the same product. Cloud collaboration made it easier for people to work together. It did not remove the effort required to gather information, make decisions, or complete processes involving several applications. That is the next area AI providers are attempting to improve. The office software landscape in 2026 Today’s productivity market includes traditional office suites, collaborative platforms, connected workspaces, and AI-first tools. The following table brings major available products into one view. It is a representative market overview rather than an exhaustive list of every office application. requirements vary. Connected workspaces and AI-first platforms are included because they overlap with parts of office productivity. They are not equivalent replacements for complete office suites. The table reveals why the market cannot be described as one direct competition. Microsoft and Google provide broad productivity ecosystems. LibreOffice and Apache OpenOffice emphasize traditional office functionality and open-source licensing. ONLYOFFICE, Collabora, and Nextcloud offer different approaches to collaboration and infrastructure control. Notion, Superhuman Docs (formerly Coda), and Airtable organize information and work in ways that extend beyond individual documents. Claude and ChatGPT Work approach some of these activities through AI-led interaction. Each category serves different needs. AI may change the boundaries between them, but that does not make their differences irrelevant. The arrival of AI-powered workspaces AI initially became visible in office software through familiar features: helping write emails, summarizing documents, creating presentation outlines, explaining spreadsheet formulas, and answering questions about business information. These tools assisted users inside existing applications. The newer approach attempts to connect more of the process. On November 10, 2026, Anthropic introduced Claude Sheets and Claude Whiteboards in beta, while making Claude Data generally available. Claude Sheets allows people and Claude to create and edit spreadsheets together, including formulas, multiple tabs, and formatting. Anthropic describes Claude Sheets as having simple spreadsheet functionality for now, and points users who need full spreadsheet features to Excel files or Claude for Excel. Claude Whiteboards supports collaborative planning, allowing teams to develop ideas, organize timelines, and turn discussions into structured work. Claude Data connects to a data source such as a warehouse or CRM and helps create dashboards and data stories. Certain advanced capabilities, including certified queries and live sharing, remain in beta. Anthropic also expanded interactive connectors so supported third-party applications can appear alongside Claude conversations. Two days later, Anthropic introduced Claude Meetings in beta. On Team and Enterprise plans, with some exclusions such as organizations that use zero data retention, Claude can join Google Meet calls, currently the only supported platform, as a visible participant, capture notes, answer questions, and help create working materials during a meeting. These capabilities expand Claude beyond answering questions and producing isolated content. They allow more work to remain connected to the conversation in which it began. However, availability and product maturity matter. A beta spreadsheet editor is not a full replacement for Excel, and a meeting assistant does not replace every function of a mature communications platform. Sources: Anthropic: Claude Sheets, Whiteboards and Data (November 10, 2026). Anthropic: Claude Meetings (November 12, 2026). Anthropic is not alone Microsoft announced a major Copilot expansion on September 25, 2026. Its direction includes creating and editing Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files directly in the Copilot experience, alongside capabilities for delegated work. Google’s September 2026 Workspace announcement described Gemini coordinating tasks across applications such as Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Chat. OpenAI introduced ChatGPT Work in July 2026 for longer tasks involving research, analysis, connected applications, and the creation of finished work products. Zoho is integrating Zia across Workplace applications and offering AI assistance for writing, analysis, and workflows. The strategies share an important ambition: help users accomplish work that previously required several disconnected actions. But they start from different positions. Microsoft and Google can build AI around established office applications, business data, identity systems, and collaboration services. Anthropic and OpenAI can pursue broader AI interfaces that work across products from multiple companies. Some relationships are collaborative as well as competitive. Microsoft, for example, added Anthropic’s Claude models as options in the Microsoft 365 Copilot Researcher agent and in Copilot Studio in September 2025. The emerging market is therefore not simply traditional software competing against AI companies. The same organizations can be suppliers, partners, and competitors. Sources: Microsoft: New Copilot (September 25, 2026). Anthropic: Claude in Microsoft 365 Copilot (September 24, 2025). Google Workspace: Agentic capabilities (September 9, 2026). OpenAI: ChatGPT release notes . Zoho: AI in Workplace . What actually changes when AI coordinates the work? Return to the monthly business report from the opening. A project manager traditionally collects figures, prepares a spreadsheet, writes a summary, and creates a presentation. The work may move through email, document storage, reporting software, and project-management tools. An AI-assisted application might help with one step, such as writing the summary or explaining a calculation. An AI-driven workspace aims to coordinate several steps from one request. For example, the manager might ask an assistant to review permitted project records, identify significant budget differences, create a report, and prepare slides for leadership. If the required connectors, permissions, and capabilities are available, the assistant could complete parts of that sequence while the manager reviews the output. This is an illustrative workflow, not a claim that every platform can perform it reliably today. The change is significant because the user’s role shifts. Rather than operating every application and transferring information between them, the user increasingly defines the outcome, provides context, examines the result, and handles decisions requiring human judgment. The distinction is between software that helps us perform individual tasks and software that can help coordinate a complete piece of work . That is the direction in which the competition is developing. What does this mean for existing software vendors? AI will not affect every product in the same way. Software primarily sold for a narrow activity, such as generating simple presentation drafts or summarizing routine meetings, could face greater competitive pressure as those functions become available inside broader AI subscriptions. A customer may question the value of paying for a separate application when an existing workspace performs the task adequately. But specialized products can remain valuable when they solve deeper problems. A business intelligence platform may provide tested business metrics, dependable data pipelines, and sophisticated permissions. A document-management system may enforce approval workflows, retention requirements, and detailed revision histories. These capabilities are not automatically reproduced when AI creates an attractive report or spreadsheet. Established office vendors also retain important advantages. Microsoft and Google have large productivity ecosystems, existing integrations, enterprise administration, and familiar document environments. Their ability to incorporate AI may strengthen those positions. Open-source and self-hosted products serve a different set of priorities. Organizations may continue choosing LibreOffice, ONLYOFFICE, Collabora, or similar software because they value local processing, software control, licensing flexibility, or infrastructure independence. AI adoption could even increase interest in these choices where organizations are concerned about sensitive data leaving their environment. For independent AI providers, the opportunity is different. If users begin work in an AI workspace rather than a particular office application, the provider of that interface may become more influential in deciding which services and tools are used to complete a task. That does not necessarily transfer ownership of business data, document formats, or underlying systems to the AI provider. It changes which part of the software experience competes most directly for the user’s attention. The longer-term business impact remains uncertain. These are plausible competitive pressures, not measured evidence of revenue losses or inevitable market consolidation. Why traditional applications still matter A financial workbook is more than a collection of numbers in cells. It may contain interconnected calculations, validations, data connections, macros, and processes that colleagues have relied on for years. An important business document may require controlled changes, legal approval, defined access permissions, and long-term retention. AI can help create or modify these materials, but the organization still needs confidence in their accuracy and integrity. There are also risks specific to AI-based work. An assistant may produce incorrect calculations, misunderstand source information, omit qualifications, or present an unsupported conclusion convincingly. Connected systems introduce additional questions. What information is the assistant authorized to read? Which actions can it perform? How are changes recorded? Can a user reverse a mistaken update? Cost also matters. A task that becomes quicker to initiate is not necessarily cheaper once model usage, corrections, human review, and administration are included. These limitations do not eliminate the value of AI. They determine where it can be used responsibly. The practical future may therefore combine AI-driven interaction with conventional applications that provide reliable editing, established formats, specialized functions, and controlled business records. What should organizations and professionals do now? Organizations do not need to replace their office suites in response to every new AI announcement. They should begin with actual work. A useful test is to select a recurring process, such as monthly management reporting, and compare the existing approach with an AI-assisted alternative. The evaluation should measure the complete task: How long does the work take from beginning to approval? Are the calculations and conclusions correct? How much human correction is necessary? Does the output remain compatible with existing systems? Are data access and permitted actions appropriately controlled? What is the total cost, including AI usage and review effort? The comparison should include AI capabilities already available in the organization’s current software. Comparing a new AI workspace against an entirely manual workflow could exaggerate its advantage. For professionals, the evolution creates a related learning opportunity. Understanding Word, Excel, Google Sheets, or other productivity applications remains useful. However, people may increasingly need to describe tasks clearly, evaluate AI-generated work, recognize errors, and understand when automated actions require approval. This does not mean every office worker needs advanced knowledge of AI models. It means that practical AI literacy, good judgment, and an understanding of the work itself are becoming more important. A person who cannot recognize a flawed financial report will not automatically make better decisions simply because AI produced it faster. The next evolution of office productivity The history of office software is a history of reducing different kinds of work. Electronic spreadsheets reduced manual recalculation. Word processors simplified document revision. Integrated suites brought common applications together. Cloud collaboration made it easier for teams to work on shared information. AI is now beginning to reduce some of the effort required to connect those activities into completed tasks. Anthropic’s November 2026 announcements are part of that evolution, alongside developments from Microsoft, Google, OpenAI, Zoho, and other providers. The winners are not yet clear. Established vendors have strong advantages, independent AI platforms are creating new possibilities, and open-source alternatives continue to address important needs. For businesses, the useful question is not whether a new AI tool can create a spreadsheet or presentation. It is whether the complete workflow becomes more accurate, secure, reliable, and economical. For decades, office software helped people perform work. Its next evolution may be defined by how effectively people can delegate work while retaining control over the result. title: How does the Curator MCP server work?
author: ScriptMasterLabs
summary: How does the Curator MCP server work? InterWorks' Curator 2026.11-02 ships an MCP server that lets an AI client such as Claude Code or Claude Desktop work directly on a Curator analytics portal — the layer that fronts Tableau, Power BI, ThoughtSpot, and Sigma content — through one endpoint, POST /curator/mcp, authenticated with a personal token that can do nothing its owner cannot do. Counted from Curator's own MCP documentation (updated November 13, 2026, read November 15, 2026), the server exposes 48 named tools: 27 read and administrative tools that a new token allows by default, and 21 content tools that change portal content and are never checked by default — the owner must opt each one in. The content surface is the consequential part: 4 page tools (create, edit content, update settings — which can publish several pages at once — and delete), 4 navigation tools, 2 theme tools, 4 file tools, 1 snapshot-restore tool, 2 REST API key tools, and 4 API relay tools. Curator's guardrails are real and unusually well documented: content tools are off by default, every call checks the owner's backend permissions at run time and is written to the Usage Log, pages and themes are snapshotted before an MCP change (the newest 25 snapshots per page or theme, kept up to 90 days), most content tools accept dry_run: true, new pages start hidden, and managed portals refuse changes outright. What Curator does not ship is a decision: 0 per-action decision scores, 0 confidence thresholds, and 0 scored approval steps are named anywhere in its documentation. title: Nvidia's Money Story Outlasts the Spy Story
author: Max Quimby
summary: Nvidia's Money Story Outlasts the Spy Story The espionage headline is fading. The governance problem is not. 📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap → A week after Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, the spy narrative that dominated the news cycle is running into a wall. The Attorney General says "no conclusions reached." The CIA says it is "not yet convinced." The Director of National Intelligence calls the spy claim "not entirely accurate and over-torqued." Even the incoming House Intelligence Committee chair, after a classified briefing, could only say: "Today, at least, I don't know." David Sacks, co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, put it bluntly : "The spy narrative is collapsing already." View original post on X → But here is what is not collapsing: a board director who sold nearly $1 billion in stock with no pre-set trading plan. A $7.5 billion pipeline of chips routed through Singapore shell companies to China. A circular financing model that has drawn comparisons to vendor lending schemes. And a succession vacuum in which the only named backup is a CFO who has never run a product organization. When the spy headline burns out — and the intelligence community's own hedging suggests it will — the market will still have to price the governance story underneath. That story is harder to dismiss, and it has numbers attached. The Intelligence Community's Walk-Back The original bombshell, first reported by the New York Times on October 29, alleged that Jensen Huang had been the target of a Chinese espionage plot through his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), CEO of Singapore-based cloud firm Megaspeed. The Financial Times cited a classified U.S. intelligence memo suggesting she had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. The allegation landed like a depth charge. Nvidia's stock dropped over 4% on the first trading day, erasing roughly $200 billion in market cap . The board opened an independent investigation. Huang emailed staff admitting to marital infidelity and pledging cooperation. The Hacker News discussion alone drew 490 points and 403 comments . View discussion on Hacker News → But then the walk-back began. CNN reported that the AG had reached no conclusions, the CIA was not yet convinced of the espionage claim, and the DNI described the initial reporting as over-torqued. China's foreign ministry called the allegations "groundless smears." President Trump defended Huang publicly. Sacks argued that the only established crime so far is the leak of the classified memo itself — and called for a leak investigation rather than a spy hunt. View original report on Benzinga → None of this exonerates anyone. Singapore confiscated Alice Huang's passport from June 2025 to February 2026 over "potential false declarations in relation to Mega Speed." The DOJ is still investigating Megaspeed's chip distribution. "No conclusions reached" is bureaucratic hedging, not absolution. But it means the market is pricing in a spy-thriller premium on a story where the intelligence community itself cannot agree on the plot. The Money Trail That Does Not Depend on Espionage Strip the espionage question away entirely. What remains is a financial story with three independent threads, each carrying its own governance risk. Thread 1: Mark Stevens' $947 Million Exit Mark Stevens, a long-serving Nvidia board director and billionaire venture capitalist, sold approximately 4.2 million shares in Q3 2026 for roughly $947 million — the largest insider sale by any U.S. corporate director that quarter. The sales ran in three batches: $411 million across August 31 to September 2, $236 million on September 3-4, and $300 million on September 18. The critical detail: no Rule 10b5-1 trading plan was flagged in the SEC filings for the initial batches. Pre-set trading plans are the standard mechanism insiders use to demonstrate that large sales are routine and not based on material non-public information. Stevens may hold a grandfathered pre-2023 arrangement that does not require the same disclosure — but in the current environment, the optics are brutal. View original report on Yahoo Finance → He also filed a Form 144 signaling a possible further sale of up to 5 million additional shares. Including earlier June sales, his total dispositions since the start of summer approach $1.35 billion. The question governance analysts are asking: what did Stevens know, and when? The spy story broke publicly on October 29. Stevens' largest batch was September 2. The board says it had no advance knowledge. The market has to decide whether it believes that. Timeline of Key Events Aug 31 – Sep 18: Mark Stevens sells ~$947M in Nvidia shares across three batches, no 10b5-1 plan flagged Oct 29: New York Times breaks the spy-plot story citing classified intelligence memo Nov 8: Nvidia board opens independent investigation; Huang emails staff admitting affair Nov 9-10: Stock drops ~10% over two sessions, erasing ~$200B+ in market cap Nov 13: David Sacks declares spy narrative "collapsing" citing AG/CIA/DNI pushback Nov 15 (today): Earnings in 2 days; congressional briefing in 3 days Thread 2: $7.5 Billion in Chips Through Singapore The Information reported that Alice Huang and her relatives built a network of companies in China and Singapore that facilitated the shipment of at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to Chinese firms — including models covered by U.S. export controls. The network allegedly moved around 240,000 H100, H200, and A100 GPUs into China through Megaspeed and related entities. CNBC's investigation into Megaspeed's footprint revealed a company whose balance sheet grew from $33 million to approximately $3 billion during 2024. Megaspeed denies any illegal chip transfers, stating it operates "fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations." Ed Zitron's detailed investigation draws on Culper Research and Bloomberg reporting to allege that Megaspeed's Singapore subsidiary, SpeedMatrix, purchased $4.8 billion in GPUs while missing circuit boards turned up at a Chinese firm (Shanghai Shuoyao) with a near-copy of Megaspeed's website and a Tencent-tenanted data center. This thread does not require the espionage allegation to be true. Even if Alice Huang never worked for Chinese intelligence, the question of whether Nvidia chips reached China through export-control-violating intermediaries stands on its own — and the DOJ investigation is ongoing. Singapore's position adds a wrinkle. The city-state has said it does not enforce unilateral export controls imposed by other countries, creating a regulatory gap that Washington may now pressure it to close. This is the same type of export-control escalation we analyzed in our coverage of how the U.S. government pulled Fable 5 — the precedent that every frontier tech company now fears. Thread 3: Circular Financing — Nvidia's Self-Reinforcing Revenue Loop The third thread predates the scandal but converges with it. Nvidia has faced persistent questions about circular financing — arrangements where the company invests in or lends to entities that are simultaneously its largest customers. The scale is staggering. Bloomberg has documented a financing web of more than $750 billion in which Nvidia invests in chip buyers who borrow to buy more chips. Jensen Huang rejected the label, calling the suggestion "ridiculous" and noting Nvidia's strategic investments total only $4.7 billion year-to-date against massive revenues. But the critics have names and numbers. Michael Burry has compared Nvidia not to Enron but to Cisco during the dot-com bubble — arguing that hyperscalers are extending GPU useful-life assumptions from 2-3 years to 5-6 years to flatter earnings. The Financial Times calls it old-fashioned vendor financing with a new label. A Hacker News thread titled "Inside the Circular Financing of the GPU Boom" drew 370 points and 182 comments, with practitioners debating whether the revenue is real or manufactured. View discussion on Hacker News → One data point cuts through the debate: the cost of insuring Nvidia's debt against default has tripled in 2026 . As we wrote in Nvidia Is the Central Bank of AI , the company has positioned itself as the backstop of GPU debt. That was a feature when the stock was climbing. It becomes a governance vulnerability when the CEO who built the system is suddenly gone. The Succession Vacuum Naval Ravikant's post captured the bull case in five words: "Jensen Huang is the Steve Jobs of Nvidia. He is irreplaceable." 85,000 likes and 4 million views suggest the market agrees — which is precisely the governance problem. View original post on X → Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran it for over three decades. There is no named successor. The most commonly cited backup is CFO Colette Kress, who has been EVP and CFO since 2013 and is deeply respected on Wall Street — but she has never run a product organization or led a hardware engineering team. A structural detail matters: Huang holds no super-voting stock. Unlike Zuckerberg at Meta or the Google founders, he can actually be removed by a standard board vote. The board expressed confidence in him and said he pledged full cooperation with the investigation. But analysts have noted that this framing — support conditional on cooperation — is the same language boards use before they pull that support. Bernstein kept its Outperform rating and $400 target. The average 12-month analyst target from 62 analysts sits at approximately $327, well above the current price near $169. Wall Street's consensus is that this is a buying opportunity. But Wall Street's consensus also assumes the governance overhang resolves cleanly — an assumption that depends on earnings (November 17) and the congressional briefing (November 18) going well. ⚠️ Contrarian Corner: Why the Bears Might Be Wrong The governance bears could be overstating the risk. If Nvidia's Q3 earnings blow past expectations on November 17 — and the data center business shows genuine demand rather than circular financing — the stock discount becomes a buying opportunity. The circular-financing critique loses force if hyperscaler capex is genuinely demand-driven rather than subsidized. And the spy narrative's collapse could actually be bullish: it removes the national-security overhang that was the biggest tail risk. Naval's "irreplaceable" framing cuts both ways — if Huang stays, the key-man premium returns instead of the key-man discount. What the Market Has to Price Now The spy story was dramatic but may prove to be a distraction. The financial engineering underneath it is mundane, documentable, and — crucially — does not require any espionage allegation to be true. Here is what the market is actually pricing: Insider selling without pre-set plans. A board director liquidated nearly $1 billion in stock in a window that, in hindsight, looks suspicious. The board says it had no advance knowledge of the scandal. The SEC filings are silent on trading-plan coverage. Export-control exposure. Whether or not Alice Huang is a spy, $7.5 billion in chips allegedly reached China through a network the DOJ is investigating. If those shipments violated export controls, Nvidia faces potential fines, license restrictions, and reputational damage in Washington at the worst possible time — right as the government debates tighter chip curbs . Circular financing risk. The company that became the central bank of AI is now being asked whether it is also lending to its own customers. Credit-default swap spreads have tripled.
